subject: Copywriting
title: The Curiosity Gap
description: Learn The Curiosity Gap in one minute.

hook.text: George Loewenstein's 'information gap' theory explains clickbait: when you know a little, you crave the rest.

buildup.text: A headline that reveals too much gets ignored. One that reveals too little feels like spam. The sweet spot is middle.

discovery.text: 'This CEO Made $1B With One Weird Trick' works because it opens a gap only the article can close.

twist.text: Curiosity headline fatigue is real. Readers now recognize the pattern and skip it. The gap closed on the gap.

climax.text: The best modern headlines create curiosity with substance, not tricks. Promise real value and deliver it.

punchline.text: Open a gap, fill it honestly. That's the updated formula.

quiz.question: Who developed the 'information gap' theory behind curiosity?

details.summary: The curiosity gap is the space between what the reader knows and what they want to know. George Loewenstein's information gap theory explains why headlines like 'The one thing successful people never do' are irresistible — the brain cannot tolerate unsatisfied curiosity and seeks resolution...
details.whyItMatters: The curiosity gap is the most exploited psychological mechanism in digital headlines. Understanding its science helps writers use it ethically while avoiding the clickbait trap.
takeaways: The curiosity gap creates discomfort the brain resolves by seeking information
Loewenstein's information gap theory explains why partial knowledge drives action
Ethical curiosity gaps promise and deliver; clickbait promises and disappoints

faq.question: What is the information gap theory?
faq.answer: George Loewenstein proposed that curiosity arises when we perceive a gap between what we know and what we want to know. This gap creates a feeling of deprivation similar to an itch. The urge to scratch — to close the gap — drives people to click, read, or investigate.

faq.question: How do you create a curiosity gap without being clickbait?
faq.answer: Provide enough context that the reader knows the topic is relevant to them, but withhold enough that they need to read to learn the specific insight. Then deliver that insight fully. The key is: always close the gap with genuinely valuable content.
